title: Directional Lighting, Sky Warp, and Multi-Zone Compositing in Photoshop: A PNW Week 2 Landscape Workflow

summary: This video presents a comprehensive post-processing workflow for landscape imagery, focused on building a cohesive composite through image selection, multi-zone lighting, and sky manipulations. The presenter emphasizes choosing frames with strong bottom-layer detail and balanced light, then creating three-dimensionality in long-lens scenes by introducing directional light and isolating zones (foreground, mid-ground, hills, and rainbow sky). Techniques span RAW adjustments, content-aware layering via history brushes, warmth and color grading, and selective masking (hard/soft brushes, clone-stamp-based warps) to integrate elements like a flaming sunrise, cloud structures, fog, and reflections. A notable portion covers sky replacement and color correction using Topaz, chromatic aberration removal, and a final glow with blur+luminosity for a dreamy finish. Throughout, the emphasis is on preserving dynamic range, guiding the viewer’s eye toward light sources, and balancing multiple layers to maintain a natural yet enhanced landscape read.

sections.title: Image selection and composition evaluation
sections.description: The presenter describes selecting images based on lighting, atmosphere, and how frames can be blended to achieve a desired result. Emphasis on choosing frames that balance bottom-dominant detail with overall composition, using a 'rule of six' heuristic to identify frames with strong bottom information and cohesive lines and colors.

sections.title: Global exposure and dynamic range balancing
sections.description: After selecting a candidate, the process moves to global adjustments: expand dynamic range, lift shadows, reduce overall exposure to prevent highlights from blowing out, and establish a baseline where highlights are controlled and the image is ready for further processing.

sections.title: Directional lighting and two-zone shaping
sections.description: The speaker explains adding directional light to a long-lens scene to create focal points and depth, with a two-zone approach (one area darker/cooler, another brighter/warmer). The right-side light direction is emphasized while the left side receives lighter diffusion.

sections.title: Layer-based warmth and contrast adjustments
concepts: exposure to zero with white addition
sections.description: Local warmth is introduced on foreground layers using white to create contrast, followed by selective warmth and saturation adjustments. The history brush is used to apply and blend changes gradually to maintain natural transitions and enhance three-dimensionality.

sections.title: Rainbow workflow and four-zone composition
concepts: four-zone approach (sky, background hills, shadows, grasses)
global adjustments and RAW vs Photoshop workflow
sections.description: The rainbow scene is treated as a four-zone composite, with careful handling of sky warmth, global saturation, and rainbow brightness. The highlight dodge tool is used to enhance the rainbow, while Topaz is used to reduce noise in the sky. The rainbow and sky are blended with a cloned sky and cloud extensions, including cloud warping and cloud cloning to extend the horizon and maintain natural texture.

sections.title: Sky replacement, chromatic aberration correction, and reflection work
sections.description: The sky is replaced and refined using Topaz denoise, followed by chromatic aberration corrections to adjacent foreground elements. The reflection is warped and blended with clone-paint techniques, ensuring the reflection matches the mountains while remaining a subtle, realistic element. This section also covers non-destructive blending using history brushes and opacity controls to preserve edge integrity.

sections.title: Closing philosophy and recap
sections.description: Brief closing remarks summarize the philosophy behind the processing approach, including a nod to future topics (coast workflows) and the guiding question: 'could the scene have happened this way?'
